_comment: Synthetic labelled set for fitting the bullet-library variant choice (issue #199). Every item is an experience or project from a synthetic eval/profiles/ profile (never personal/), its variants are alternative phrasings of that item's own bullets, each angled toward a role track, and each case is one job (a title from eval/jd_dataset and requirements written the way a host would extract them) asked about one item's approved variants. The label is the set of acceptable variants (`best`, empty when none fits) and the variants that clearly do not fit (`poor_fit`). Labels are planner-reviewed, pending user spot-check. Recordings of Jev's answers are in recordings.json; re-run `python eval/fit_library_thresholds.py analyze` after correcting a label.

cases.rationale: Esri wants predictive models; the churn classifier is exactly that. The report automation shows no modelling.
The fraud-monitoring role asks for dashboards stakeholders use; only the dashboard bullet shows one.
Tebra asks for real-time pipelines; the Kafka-to-Postgres connector is one. The Terraform bullet is infrastructure.
Edge ML on signals: the autoencoder anomaly detector on accelerometer streams is the match.
A full stack role wants an application with a UI and a database; the Next.js and Postgres bullet shows both.
A front end role wants web application work; the Next.js app is it. Deployment and uptime show no front end work.
The backend role asks for built software; the autograder is a built tool. Grading and running labs are teaching.
A junior data engineer moves and cleans data in SQL and Python; the cleaning bullet does. A statistical model is not that.
Both phrasings of the forecasting bullet show predictive modelling; the dbt consolidation does not.
Training and tuning forecasting models fits an ML role in either phrasing; the dbt layer is data modelling.
The role asks for data quality and a statistical foundation: cleaning (either phrasing) and the mixed-effects models both serve it. A plotting toolkit is neither.
Pipelines and infrastructure as code on AWS: the Airflow retraining schedule and the Terraform SageMaker stack both fit. Demand modelling does not.
Backend services and APIs: the Go service (either phrasing) and the GraphQL resolvers both fit; the end-to-end tests fit less.
A full stack role asks for REST APIs and automated tests: the GraphQL resolvers and the Cypress tests both fit.
A junior pipeline role: the nightly Spark job and the tested dbt models both show pipelines and quality; the Kafka backfill is a closer second.
Reports stakeholders use, and findings shared with non-technical colleagues: the cohort report and the A/B readouts both fit.
A front end role; none of the data science bullets show front end work.
Chip timing analysis; none of the ML infrastructure bullets touch hardware design.

The SageMaker training environment repeats cloud and machine learning terms, but Terraform provisioning shows no modelling; the demand models do.
